(See Morphisms, Definition <REF_0001>).
Let <MATH_0001> be a morphism of schemes.
Let <MATH_0002> be a quasi-coherent <MATH_0003>-module.
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> Let <MATH_0004>. We say <MATH_0005> is
<TEXTITOPEN_0001>flat over <MATH_0006> at <MATH_0007><TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if <MATH_0008>
is a flat <MATH_0009>-module.
This uses the map <MATH_0010> to
think of <MATH_0011> as a <MATH_0012>-module.
<STRUCT_0003> Let <MATH_0013>. We say <MATH_0014> is <TEXTITOPEN_0002>flat at <MATH_0015><TEXTITCLOSE_0002>
if <MATH_0016> is flat.
<STRUCT_0004> We say <MATH_0017> is <TEXTITOPEN_0003>flat<TEXTITCLOSE_0003> if it is flat at all points of <MATH_0018>.
<STRUCT_0005> A morphism <MATH_0019> that is flat and surjective is sometimes
said to be <TEXTITOPEN_0004>faithfully flat<TEXTITCLOSE_0004>.
<STRUCT_0006>

<STRUCT_0001>
Once again, here is a list of results:
<STRUCT_0002>
<STRUCT_0003> The property (of a morphism) of being flat is, by fiat,
local in the Zariski topology on the source and the target.
<STRUCT_0004> Open immersions are flat. (This is clear because it induces isomorphisms
on local rings.)
<STRUCT_0005> Flat morphisms are stable under base change and composition.
Morphisms, Lemmas <REF_0001> and
<REF_0002>.
<STRUCT_0006> If <MATH_0001> is flat, then the pullback functor
<MATH_0002> is exact.
This is immediate by looking at stalks.
<STRUCT_0007> Let <MATH_0003> be a morphism of schemes, and assume <MATH_0004>
is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. In this case
if the functor <MATH_0005> is exact then <MATH_0006> is flat.
(Proof omitted. Hint: Use
Properties, Lemma <REF_0003> to see that
<MATH_0007> has ``enough'' ideal sheaves and use the characterization of
flatness in Algebra, Lemma <REF_0004>.)
<STRUCT_0008>
